subtype: Loyalty to family versus honesty with self [Actor]
passage:
Aparna, can I tell you something ugly? Every first of the month, when my salary comes, I send most of it home. Nanu's house repairs, my brother's college fees, the old loan. I do it gladly. Mostly.
But last week the admission letter for the evening design course came, and I just sat on the bus holding it. I couldn't afford it. Again. And I felt this flash of, why is it always me? Then straight away I felt terrible for thinking that about the people who raised me.
So I did something new. I called Maa, and instead of saying 'all fine', I said, 'Maa, I love you all. I'll keep sending money for the fees. But I need to keep a little every month for myself, for this course.'
She was quiet. Then she said, 'Ankita, why didn't you tell us sooner?'

qa.q: What came for Ankita last week?
qa.a: The admission letter for the evening design course.

qa.q: What two feelings hit Ankita on the bus, and why?
qa.a: Ankita felt a flash of resentment, 'why is it always me', and then guilt for thinking that about the people who raised Ankita.

qa.q: What choice did Ankita make on the call with Maa?
qa.a: Instead of saying 'all fine', Ankita kept paying for the fees but clearly set aside a little each month for the course.

qa.q: How might Maa feel hearing about the course only now?
qa.a: Maa might feel sad that Ankita carried this in silence, and perhaps relieved to finally know what Ankita wants.

grounding: Shows a young adult who sends money home and delays their own wants, feels resentment and guilt together, and names a clear limit.

subtype: Loyalty to family versus honesty with self [Actor]
passage:
I've shared a room with Anjali at the working women's hostel for two years, so I know her Sunday routine. Video call with her parents at nine. Money transfer at ten. Then she goes quiet for hours.
She has been saving for a scooter since last Diwali. Last Sunday her brother asked for more money for a new phone, and I watched her say 'of course' in a bright voice and then press her forehead against the cupboard after the call.
I don't know exactly what she felt. It looked like love and anger fighting.
On Monday she asked me, 'Gopika, is it wrong to say no sometimes?' I said I didn't think so.
That night I heard her on the phone, voice shaky but clear: 'I'll send for the fees. Not for the phone. I need to keep something for me too.'

qa.q: What has Anjali been saving for since last Diwali?
What did Anjali pressing her forehead against the cupboard suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggested she was holding back hurt and anger after saying 'of course' to her brother, torn between love and resentment.

qa.q: What choice did Anjali make on the phone that night?
qa.a: She kept sending money for the fees but said no to the phone, clearly saying she needed to keep something for herself.

qa.q: How might Anjali's brother react to hearing 'Not for the phone'?
qa.a: He might feel disappointed or surprised at first, but a calm, clear limit could also help him see what his sister has been carrying.

grounding: Shows, through a roommate's eyes, a young adult who supports her family while delaying her own wants, feels love and resentment together, and sets a clear limit.
